authoringProvenance.author: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Pro — candidate authoring assistant

items.prompt: A single-pass validator opens nested contexts and must close the most recently opened context that is still unresolved. Which state discipline matches that requirement?
constraints: Only unresolved contexts need to remain available.
A closing event always applies to the most recently opened unresolved context.

options.text: Keep unresolved contexts in a queue and inspect the front.
Keep unresolved contexts on a stack and inspect the top.
Use recursion; an explicit data structure cannot represent this rule.

feedback.reason: The decisive signal is “most recently opened and still unresolved,” which is exactly a LIFO boundary.

blocks.text: Each opening event pushes one unresolved context. A closing event must compare against the top because no earlier context may close while a newer nested context remains open. A queue exposes the oldest context and therefore reverses the required dependency. Recursion can internally use a call stack, but it is not required; the learning decision is the LIFO state rule itself.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.use_queue: A queue is plausible because it also stores pending work, but it exposes the oldest pending context. It becomes valid only when the next action must serve arrival order rather than close nested work.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.use_recursion_only: Recursion can create LIFO call frames, but the problem does not require recursive control flow. An explicit stack is sufficient whenever the input is processed iteratively.

items.prompt: Select all statements that correctly describe why a stack is sufficient for a newest-first unresolved-state process.
constraints: A resolved record is never needed again.
Each record is pushed at most once.

options.text: The next decision depends on the most recently added unresolved record.
The oldest unresolved record must always be processed first.
The same pushed record may be popped repeatedly without being pushed again.
A record may be removed permanently once it is resolved.
Every record must remain stored for the entire scan.

feedback.reason: A stack is sufficient because only the newest unresolved record is actionable, and resolved records leave the state permanently.

blocks.text: The stack represents the unresolved suffix of the process, not a full historical log. Pushing introduces a record once; popping removes that particular stack entry once. Oldest-first service would require queue semantics, while retaining every processed record is unnecessary unless a separate audit requirement exists. This one-way lifecycle is also the basis for later amortized analysis.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.oldest_first: Oldest-first service is a FIFO contract. It would justify a queue, not a stack.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.keep_every_record: A full audit log may retain every record, but that is a separate requirement. The LIFO decision state needs only unresolved records.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.repeat_pop_same_record: After an entry is popped it is no longer in the stack. It can be removed again only if a new entry is pushed.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.last_unresolved: Without the newest-first dependency, LIFO is not the decisive state rule.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.discard_resolved: If resolved records never leave, the structure is being used as history rather than as the minimal unresolved state.

items.prompt: A process opens context A, then opens context B, and then receives one generic close event. Which context must be closed first under a valid nested-state contract?

options.text: Close A, because A entered the process first.
Close both A and B because a stack stores all active contexts together.
Close B, because B is the most recently opened unresolved context.

feedback.reason: Nested resolution closes B first because the most recent unresolved context is on top.

blocks.text: After opening A and then B, the unresolved stack is [A, B] with B on top. Closing A first would cross the nesting boundary and leave B suspended inside a context that no longer exists. The stack may contain multiple active contexts, but one close event resolves exactly the top entry unless the contract explicitly states otherwise.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.close_a: Arrival order is a queue signal. It becomes valid only for oldest-first work, not nested closure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.close_both: The presence of multiple entries does not make one event resolve all of them. Bulk closure would need an explicit separate rule.

items.prompt: A support system must always process the request that has waited the longest. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: A stack is still equivalent because both structures remove one pending request.
This is a FIFO boundary, so a queue matches the decision rule.
The requirement implies recursive processing rather than a queue.

feedback.reason: The decisive requirement is oldest-first service, which is FIFO rather than LIFO.

blocks.text: Both stacks and queues can hold pending requests, but their removal order is not interchangeable. A stack would repeatedly favor the newest request and could starve older work. Recursion says nothing about which pending request should be chosen. The transfer boundary is the service order, not the existence of a container.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.stack_boundary: Removing one item does not make order irrelevant. A stack chooses the newest pending request, which violates the stated contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.recursion_boundary: Recursive control flow does not establish oldest-first service. The required state discipline is a queue.

items.prompt: An editor processes a flat stream of commands and must undo the most recent committed command. Which implementation conclusion follows from the requirement alone?

options.text: The feature requires recursive functions because every stack operation is recursion.
The commands must be kept in monotonic value order before undo can work.
An explicit stack of inverse commands or prior states is sufficient.

feedback.reason: Undo needs newest-first history, not recursive decomposition or numeric monotonic order.

blocks.text: Each committed command can push either an inverse operation or the state needed to restore the previous version. Undo pops the newest entry and applies it. The command stream may be processed iteratively, and command values need not be ordered. A call stack is one possible runtime mechanism, but it is not the product-level decision being trained.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.recursion_required: Recursion is plausible because language runtimes use a call stack, but undo history is explicit application state and can be managed iteratively.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.retain_all_in_monotonic_order: Monotonic order is useful for dominated-candidate problems, not for chronological undo. Undo order is determined by recency.

items.prompt: A navigation controller is on page C. Before visiting B it stored A, and before visiting C it stored B. The back-history stack is therefore [A, B] with B on top. What happens after two Back actions?
constraints: Each Back action pops exactly one history entry and makes it current.

options.text: The controller restores B, then A.
The controller restores A, then B.
The controller restores B twice because B was most recent.

feedback.reason: Each Back action consumes one newest history entry, so B is restored before A.

blocks.text: The first pop removes B and makes it current; the second pop removes A. The same stack entry cannot be popped twice, and a queue would reverse the navigation order. This transfer works because Back is explicitly newest-first. A forward-history feature would require a separate stack or another state contract.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.restore_a_then_b: That is FIFO history replay. It would skip the most recent prior page.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.restore_b_twice: Once B is popped, that entry is gone. Repeating B would require pushing a new B entry.

items.prompt: An editor commits commands C1, C2, and C3. Undo must remove the most recently committed command that has not already been undone. Which state discipline matches?

options.text: A stack of committed commands, with the newest command on top.
A queue that removes C1 first because it arrived first.
A sorted list ordered by command text rather than commit time.
A set, because any undone command is equally eligible.

feedback.reason: Undo targets the newest still-active command, which is a direct LIFO requirement.

blocks.text: After C1, C2, C3, the first undo must remove C3, then C2, then C1. A stack stores only the unresolved history in the order needed by the next action. A queue, sorted order, or unordered set loses the required recency relation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.arrival_queue: FIFO would undo the oldest command first, reversing the required history order.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorted_commands: Lexical or numeric sorting does not represent commit recency.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.random_set: A set does not expose which eligible command was committed most recently.

items.prompt: A parser reads open(A), open(B), close(B), close(A). Which recognition fact makes a stack sufficient for validating the nested structure?

options.text: Each closer must match the most recently opened context that has not yet been closed.
Each closer must match the oldest open context so the structure is processed FIFO.
Each closer matches the numerically or lexically largest opener, regardless of nesting.
Open contexts have no order, so any pending opener may be removed.

feedback.reason: Nested closure is newest-first: the latest unresolved opener owns the next legal close.

blocks.text: After open(A), open(B), B is the top unresolved context, so close(B) is legal and removes B. A then becomes the top and can be closed. The stack stores the unmatched contexts; it does not need to retain already resolved openers.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.oldest_unmatched_opener: Oldest-first would pair close(B) with A and violate proper nesting.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.largest_label: Labels do not determine nesting ownership; opening order does.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.all_openers_equal: The nesting contract makes the most recent unresolved opener uniquely eligible.

items.prompt: A support system must process tickets in arrival order, oldest first, even when newer tickets are waiting. What is the correct classification?

options.text: A FIFO queue is the matching state discipline.
A LIFO stack is required because every pending item has a last position.
A nesting stack is required because tickets can be processed one at a time.
A monotonic stack is required because ticket age is ordered.

feedback.reason: Oldest-first service is FIFO, so it is a boundary case that should not be mislabeled as LIFO merely because a container is needed.

blocks.text: A stack would return the newest pending ticket and violate the service contract. Nothing in the requirement asks for nested resolution, nearest-value dominance, or a most-recent rollback. Recognizing the requested order is more decisive than the presence of a push-like insertion operation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.stack_lifo: LIFO serves the newest ticket first, opposite to the stated oldest-first policy.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.nested_stack: Sequential processing does not imply nested unresolved contexts.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.monotonic_stack: No candidate domination or nearest-value query is present; ticket age is simply FIFO order.

items.prompt: Select all problem signals that support an ordinary LIFO stack rather than a queue or monotonic stack.

options.text: The next action always targets the most recently opened or unresolved context.
Undo removes the latest committed state that has not already been undone.
The next action must process the oldest pending item.
Candidates may be permanently removed because an ordered successor dominates them for a nearest-value query.

feedback.reason: Ordinary LIFO follows recency, while FIFO follows age and monotonic stacks add an ordered-dominance invariant.

blocks.text: Nested validation and undo both need the newest unresolved or reversible entry. Oldest waiting work is queue behavior. Permanently removing dominated candidates is a separate monotonic-stack proof and requires more than simple recency.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.oldest_waiting: Oldest-first is FIFO and conflicts with newest-first resolution.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.dominated_candidates: This signal points to a monotonic stack, whose ordered candidate invariant is distinct from ordinary LIFO.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.latest_unresolved: The newest pending context is exactly the entry exposed by a stack.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.undo_latest: Rollback of the most recent pending state is a direct LIFO transfer.

items.prompt: Which interaction is a natural LIFO-stack signal?

options.text: Undo browser navigation by returning to the most recently visited page first.
Serve customers in arrival order.
Return numbers in numeric order.
Answer range sums with cumulative boundaries.

feedback.reason: Back navigation removes the newest history entry before older entries.

blocks.text: The defining signal is last-in-first-out reversal of recent state. A queue matches arrival order, while sorting and prefix sums solve different relations.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorted_numbers: Numeric order is not recency order.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.range_sum: Range aggregation uses prefix state, not LIFO history.

items.prompt: Why does nested-delimiter validation require LIFO state?

options.text: The most recently opened delimiter must be the first one closed.
The earliest opening delimiter always closes first.
Any matching opening anywhere in the stack may close.
Delimiters are closed in alphabetic order.

feedback.reason: Proper nesting is a last-opened, first-closed constraint.

blocks.text: The stack top is the only legal opening counterpart for a closing token. Allowing an older match accepts crossing structures.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.first_open_closes: That is not nested closure order.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.any_match: A deeper unmatched opening cannot be skipped.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorted_delimiters: Delimiter type order is not lexical.

items.prompt: What must an undo stack expose when a user asks to undo once?

options.text: The most recently stored reversible state, then remove or consume it.
The first snapshot ever stored.
Every snapshot at once, even for one undo.
A state that has not yet been recorded.

feedback.reason: Undo reverses the latest action first.

blocks.text: A second undo reveals the prior snapshot. Snapshot ownership and branch behavior must be explicit if new actions occur after an undo.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.all_snapshots: One undo consumes one latest action under the usual contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.future_state: Undo cannot restore a state never recorded.

items.prompt: Which task pattern uses a stack because the latest unresolved item should be matched when new input arrives?

options.text: Resolve the most recent pending boundary or candidate when a qualifying event appears.
Always resolve the oldest pending item first.
Sort all events before any state is created.
Answer each item without retaining unresolved state.

feedback.reason: The stack top represents the latest unresolved candidate that a new event can close or resolve.

blocks.text: Nested structures, undo history, and nearest-boundary problems share this LIFO signal even though their payloads differ.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.global_sort: Some online resolutions cannot be deferred to a global sort.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.independent_lookup: The task explicitly needs unresolved history.

contrastSets.transferBoundary: Use an ordinary stack when the next action targets the most recent unresolved state; use a monotonic stack only when an ordered candidate frontier permits permanent domination and suffix removal.
A stack exposes the newest unresolved entry, whereas a queue exposes the oldest; the operation trace must follow the order promised by the task rather than the container name.
Nested validation needs the most recent unmatched opener; monotonic stacks instead discard dominated candidates under an ordered nearest-value invariant.
